title: Evaluating Neighbor Discovery Time in Wireless Sensor Networks
author: Passos, Trabbold, et al.

steps.title: Set simulation parameters
steps.instruction: Provide the two node schedules (A and B), the total number of repetitions, the discovery success probability p, the number of subslots per slot s, and select the discovery mode (unidirectional or bidirectional).

steps.title: Create subslot schedule
steps.instruction: Generate the augmented schedule by subdividing every original slot into s equal subslots.

steps.title: Run each simulation repetition
steps.instruction: For each repetition, randomly initialise node A’s slot, choose a clock offset between A and B, locate the next suitable subslot according to the discovery mode, test discovery success with a uniform random draw, repeat offset selection on failure, and record elapsed subslots.

substeps.instruction: Randomly select an initial slot for node A.
Randomly select an offset between the internal clocks of A and B.

If discovery mode is bidirectional, find the next subslot where both A and B are active and A occupies the first subslot of its slot; otherwise (unidirectional) find the next subslot where both are active and either A or B occupies the first subslot of its slot.
Draw X from a uniform distribution on [0,1] and declare discovery successful if X ≤ p.
If discovery is not successful, return to the offset selection step.
Store the number of subslots elapsed since the start of this repetition in a samples array.

steps.title: Compute estimated NDT
steps.instruction: After completing the requested number of repetitions, average the stored subslot counts and divide the result by s to obtain the estimated neighbor discovery time (NDT).

description: Several works in the literature evaluate the NDT of asynchronous duty-cycle schedules by means of either numerical simulators or mathematical models [6,7]. Perhaps the seminal work to explore these approaches was [4]. In essence, both approaches compute an average considering all possible combinations of rotations between the schedule and itself, as well as the starting slot for the transmitting node – i.e., the slot in which the transmitting node decides to communicate with its neighbor. For a given combination of rotation and starting slot, the model or simulator counts the number of slots until the first encounter opportunity. Given a schedule with a length of n slots, there are n2 such combinations. Some models and simulators are simplified and instead consider only a subset of those combinations, thus yielding an approximation for the NDT. Among those, probabilistic simulators perform a certain number of repetitions, which consist of randomly choosing a rotation and starting slot, and obtaining a sample for the NDT. Later, those samples are averaged to obtain an approximation for the NDT. Those probabilistic simulators are particularly useful in cases where one wishes to also take into account a non-zero frame loss probability – i.e., when multiple encounter opportunities may be needed because the transmitted frames can be lost. For validating the proposed subslot-based methodology, we used the numerical simulator described in the previous section and performed simulations considering different scenarios and parameter variations. Notice that when the number of subslots per slot s is 1, the subslot-based methodology is equivalent to the slot-based methodology. Each point shown in the following graphs corresponds to the average NDT considering 1000,000 repetitions of the corresponding simulation.
